translations.text: Thus a wise father, a man wise of mind, old in [?] excellences, taught his noble son with words firm in wisdom, so that he might prosper well:

"Always do what is fitting, and your deeds will prosper. God will always be your lord and help in every good thing, and an enemy to the other, the man of worse deeds. Accustom yourself to the better; carry this out with courage always, as long as you live."
Love your father and mother with your heart, and every kinsman, if he holds the Lord dear.
Always be respectful to your elders and fair of speech to them, and keep your teachers dear in your heart and mind, those who most eagerly urge you toward good."
The wise father addressed his son again a second time: "Hold to this with zeal!

Do not commit crime, and never allow wickedness to your friend or kinsman, in case the Lord accuses you of being a witness to the sin. He will repay you with punishment, just as he repays the others with prosperity."
A third time the man wise in thought taught his son with the thoughts of his heart:

"Never in all your life keep company with a worse man in any [?] counsel. Instead, always take as your companion in talk one who is wise in counsel about stories and teachings. As for power, let it be as it may."
A fourth time the father again taught his dearly loved son, so that he would remember this:
"Do not betray a close friend, but always keep faith with him with right and fitting conduct. Carry this out with courage, so that you never become false to your friend."

A fifth time the father again began to teach his son with the thoughts of his heart: "Guard yourself against drunkenness and foolish words, wickedness in the mind and lies in the mouth, anger and envy and the love of a woman.
For the man who goes off into the love of a woman, a strange maiden, will often have to go about in shame.
There is always the prospect of sins there, of hateful disgrace, long enmity with God, and overflowing boastfulness. Always be wise in speech, wary of desire, a guardian of your words."
A sixth time the dear one again began, with a kindly thought, to teach his son:
"Learn eagerly what is good or evil, and always tell them apart with a sharp mind in your heart, and always choose the better for yourself."
The choice is always set before you. If your mind is good, wisdom dwells within, and you clearly know what evil is. Hold out against it with courage, and always cherish good in your spirit."
A seventh time the father, a wise man, taught his son and told the young one many things:
"Seldom does a wise man rejoice free from sorrow; likewise a fool is seldom [?] sorrowful about his future fate, unless he knows of a feud."
A man firm in wisdom must think in his breast and be careful in speech, not loud in clamour."
An eighth time the old father began to exhort his son with gentle words:

"Learn teaching that is fit to be learned. Accustom yourself to wisdom. Keep the Creator of hosts as your hope, and the remembrance of the saints, and always keep truth [?] for victory when you say anything."
A ninth time the old man spoke; the aged sage told his son many things:

"There are not many peoples now who are willing to keep the ancient writings. Instead their mind decays, their courage cools, and the nation grows idle. They care nothing for it, even though they do wrong against the command of the Lord."

"Many a one will pay for it with torment of the soul. But let your mind keep from now on the ancient writings and the Lord's judgments, which here in every nation men let sink away more than would be right for themselves."
A tenth time, full of grievous sorrows, the old man again began to teach his son:

"He enjoys wisdom who, for love of his soul, always guards himself in his heart against the stains of words and deeds, and does what is true. Every one of his gifts will be increased by God, and he will be rich in powers, when he flees wickedness."
Never let anger, rising high in your heart, overpower you and defile the depths with a surge of fierce words, but a man guards himself against that in a steadfast mind.
A man must be firm in wisdom and moderate, prudent of mind, sharp in his thoughts, eager for wisdom, so that he may win prosperity among men.
Do not be too ready to find fault, nor double-tongued, and do not let men seem too contemptible in your mind, but be kindly; carry a heart light in its thoughts in your breast.
So, my son, remember the wise father's teaching, and always keep yourself from sins."
